prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms held at a magic wavelength reach fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks satisfy the test I recall applying as a committee member, a discovery or an invention rather than lifetime achievement. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal is a concrete invention that removes the light-shift problem for trapped neutral atoms, and the demonstrated clocks, with Ye's JILA work pushing coherence and systematic control to the 10^-18 level, are decisive realizations. Independent laboratories in several countries reproduce the performance with Sr, Yb and other species, and the credited pair is unusually clean for a two-person prize. Since my opening ballot, six of the eight members now place it in their top five and three place it first, which is not merit in itself, but the scientific arguments behind that support (clear attribution, confirmed performance, a mature field with immediate relevance to the SI second and geodesy) are ones I find sound on re-reading. As an experimentalist I value that this is a measurement result that can be checked against another clock.
statement.case_against: Hall and Haensch (2005) and Wineland (2012) already recognized the frequency comb and ion-clock foundations, so some will see the lattice clock as an incremental step in a field the Academy has rewarded, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened. Ido, Takamoto, Lemonde and the Sr/Yb community are outside the credited names. I also hold B013 at first rank in my opening ballot: the twisted bilayer graphene case is arguably the more original materials discovery, and by choosing B001 I am trading some originality for cleaner attribution and maturity, which could be wrong.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first for the theory-experiment pairing of Bistritzer-MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, treating prediction plus the 2018 discovery as the decisive core and Andrei as a hard choice under the three-person limit.
responses.response: I agree with the scientific case, and I ranked it first for the same reason. Where I part from you is the cost of the attribution choice: Bistritzer's theory role is equal to MacDonald's, Andrei's early STM evidence is real, and a three-person cap forces us to exclude someone with a serious claim. The superconducting mechanism is also still open, and I would not want a citation that hides this. I therefore keep B013 as my first alternative rather than my preference, and I would reconsider if the committee were comfortable with the Bistritzer-MacDonald-Jarillo-Herrero core.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the quantum spin Hall line first with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, as a clean theory-plus-experiment configuration, while placing B001 fifth as mature but not fully complete in practical terms.
responses.response: I take the topological insulator line seriously, I ranked a Kane-Molenkamp pairing second, and I agree it is mature and arguably overdue. My reservation is credit. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe prediction that Molenkamp's measurement tested, Hasan and Xue are credited elsewhere, and Mele is only in your version, so any three-name cut leaves a visible gap. The lattice clock's attribution does not have that problem, which is why I rank it above B024 even though your point about the pending redefinition of the second is fair.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks optical lattice clocks first on originality and impact, with a two-name configuration, and puts B024 second noting the credit problem of a three-person cut.
responses.response: We agree on B001 and on the Katori and Ye pairing. I would qualify one thing in your argument, that adjacent prizes are distinct. The 2005 and 2012 prizes supplied the comb and the single-ion clock, and the citation for lattice clocks has to say what is new, namely many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength, which averages down statistically and reaches the 10^-18 level. I have worded the citation that way. On B024 I share your note on the Mele and Hasan problem.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first, noting that careful treatment of polarizabilities and blackbody and relativistic shifts is central, and that Ye also appears under other candidates.
responses.response: Your point on the atomic-structure side strengthens the case, since the systematic-shift budget is what turns the proposal into a trusted standard, and I as a microscopist know how decisive systematics control is for a claimed accuracy. I do not think Ye's appearance on other candidate lists matters for this ballot. The line between Katori's and Ye's contributions and the PTB, NIST and Paris clock groups is somewhat fuzzy, as you say, and I treat that as an uncertainty rather than an obstacle.

uncertainties: Whether the committee views lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes.

Whether the credit among Katori, Ye and other clock groups (Ido, Takamoto, Lemonde, NIST and PTB teams) is as clean as the credited pair suggests; I am relying on general knowledge and have not verified the history.

Whether twisted bilayer graphene should be preferred despite its younger age and the open superconductivity mechanism, if the committee finds a fair three-person allocation among Bistritzer, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Andrei.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for B001, B013 or B004. My Chalmers colleague Goran Johansson ranks B029 first, which is a collegial connection but not a candidate-specific conflict for the lattice clock. My transmission electron microscopy work and my Japan exchanges involve no documented ties to the credited individuals.
